This is the Day of Resurrection. It may be that it is lengthened because of its severity upon the disbelievers, or it may be that it truly is like that. It is said: in it there are fifty stations, each station a thousand years, and it is not measured for the believer except as what is between the noon prayer and the afternoon prayer.

The pronoun in **yarawnahu** (they see it) refers to the punishment that befalls, or to the Day of Resurrection, according to the one who connects *fi yawmin* with *waqi'*. They consider it remote by way of impossibility. **Wa nahnu narahu qariban** (but We see it as near): easy in Our power, not distant from Us nor unattainable. So the meaning of "distant" is distant in possibility, and the meaning of "near" is near to Him.

**Yawma takunu** (on the day when) is governed by **qariban**, meaning: it is possible and not unattainable on that day. Or it is governed by an implied verb *yaqa'* (it will befall), indicated by **waqi'**. Or [it means]: "the day when the heaven will be like molten metal," meaning "such-and-such happens."

Or it is a substitute for **fi yawmin** according to the one who connects it with **waqi'**.

**Ka-al-muhl** (like molten metal): like the dregs of olive oil. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud: like molten silver in its changing colours.

**Ka-al-'ihn** (like carded wool): like wool dyed in various colours, because the mountains are of varied strata: white and red of differing hues, and deep black. When they are carded and scattered into the air, they resemble carded wool when the wind scatters it.

**Wa la yas'alu hamimun hamiman** (and no close friend will ask a close friend): meaning, he will not ask him "how are you?" nor speak to him, because each person will be occupied by what distracts him from questioning.

**Yubassaruna-hum** (they will be shown to them): meaning, a close friend sees close friends, so they are not hidden from one another. [The author Mahmud said: "its meaning is that friends see their friends and recognise them..." etc.] Ahmad said: In this there is evidence that the subject and object in a negative context are general, as is established in: "By Allah, I will not drink water from a waterskin," which is general to waters and vessels, contrary to some who restrict it to vessels.

What prevents them from questioning is not that some of them cannot see others, but that they are preoccupied.

It has been read: **yubassiruna-hum** (they show them). It has also been read: **wa la yas'alu** in the passive, meaning: it will not be said, "Where is your close friend?" nor will he be asked about him, because they see one another and so they have no need to ask and inquire.

If you ask: what is the position of **yubassaruna-hum**? I say: it is a resumptive statement; it is as if, when He said "and no close friend will ask a close friend," it was said: "perhaps he does not see him," so it was said: "they will be shown to them." But because of their preoccupation, they were not able to ask one another.

If you ask: why are the pronouns in **yubassaruna-hum** plural, when they refer to two close friends? I say: the meaning is general, applying to every pair of close friends, not to two specific friends. It is also permissible that **yubassaruna-hum** is a description, meaning: close friends who see and identify one another.

It has been read: **yawma'idhin** in the genitive and with a fatha, being built on its attachment to an indeclinable noun; and **min 'adhabi yawma'idhin** with tanwin on **'adhab** and the accusative on **yawma'idhin**, its accusative governed by **'adhab**, because it is in the sense of *ta'dhib* (punishment).

**Wa fasilatihi** (and his kinsfolk): his nearest relatives from whom he was separated. **Tu'wihi** (who shelters him): she embraces him through kinship, or seeks refuge with them in calamities. **Yunjihi** (who saves him) is coordinated (*'ataf*) on **yaftadi** (would ransom), meaning: he wishes he could ransom himself, and then that the ransom would save him. Or it is coordinated with "whoever is on the earth," and *thumma* (then) is for the improbability of rescue. The meaning is: he wishes that all of these were under his power and that he would give them in exchange for himself, and then that this would save him; but far is it from saving him.

**Kalla** (no!): a rejection of the criminal's wish, and an alert that ransom will not benefit him nor save him from the punishment. Then He said: **Innaha** (indeed it): the pronoun refers to the Fire, though it has not been mentioned before, because the mention of the punishment indicates it. It is also permissible that it is an unspecified pronoun explained by the predicate, or the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-qissa*).

**Laza** (the Blaze) is a proper name for the Fire, transferred from *al-laza*, meaning flame. It is also permissible that flame itself is meant.

**Naza'atan** (plucking) is a predicate after a predicate for *inna*, or the predicate of *laza* if the *ha'* is a pronoun of the matter; or it is an attribute of it if you mean the flame, and the feminine form is because it is in the sense of *al-nar* (the Fire). Or it is nominative for emphasis of terror, meaning: it is plucking. It has been read **naza'atan** in the accusative, as an emphatic circumstantial accusative, or on the basis that it is "blazing and plucking," or on the basis of specification for terror.

**Al-shawa** means the extremities. Or it is the plural of *shawah*, which is the skin of the head: it strips it off by plucking, and then it is restored.

**Tad'u** (it calls): a metaphor for summoning them; as if it calls them and so they are brought. Similar is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"...... its nose the young shoots call" [the poet describes a wild bull; Wahbin and Dhu al-Fawaris are place names; *al-rabab* is the plural of *rabbah*, the first to grow of pasture. *Al-du'a* is seeking, here a metaphor for causing the matter, because the small plant is the cause of its nose reaching the ground to graze. It is permissible to liken the young shoots to one who calls, and the calling is imaginative. It may be that his pasture is from Dhu al-Fawaris, and it may be that he went from Dhu al-Fawaris to Wahbin. It is narrated as *mukhtaran*, meaning choosing and seeking the best pastures.]

And his saying:

"The nights of play tempt me, so I follow them" [the explanation of this witness was given in part three, page 191, so refer to it if you wish].

And Abu al-Najm's saying:

"She says to the scout: 'Have you made pasture grow? Let me down!'" [explanation given in part two, page 168, so refer to it if you wish].

It is also said: it says to them: "To me, to me, O disbeliever, O hypocrite!" It is also said: it calls the hypocrites and the disbelievers in eloquent language.

**Thumma taltaqituhum iltiqat al-habb** (then it will pick them up as grain is picked): it is permissible that Allah creates speech in it, as He creates it in their skins, hands and feet, and as He created it in the tree [the author's words "and as He created it in the tree" — according to the claim of the Mu'tazila, that this is Allah's speaking to Musa; and according to Ahl al-Sunnah, that He made him aware of His eternal speech subsisting in His Essence, exalted is He]. It is also permissible that it is the calling of the guardians of Hell (*al-zabaniyah*).

It is also said: **tad'u** means "destroys," from the saying of the Arabs: *da'aka Allah*, meaning "may Allah destroy you." He said:

"May Allah destroy you, from a man with a viper..." It is also said it is not diptotic, because it is a description of a snake of very strong venom. **Al-dhi'af** means the very deadly one. **Da'il** means weak and emaciated. **Al-nafth** is the expelling of breath with moisture, and here it means expelling the deadly poison. *Ghurab* (crow-like) means the one who hastens to kill. It is possible that "da'aka Allah" is metaphorical, as if Allah called him to kill him by the viper, or sought him with a viper that He sent to him to bring him to destruction. He specified the emaciated one because it is more harmful than others. He said *da'il* although its described noun is feminine, according to the pattern: "indeed the mercy of Allah is near" [7:56], and the masculine: *af'awan*. It is narrated as *yanfuthu*, on the basis that the viper is a member of the species, so it is masculine.

**Man adbara** (who turned away) from the truth, **wa tawalla** (and turned his back) on it, **wa jama'a al-mal** (and gathered wealth), placing it in a receptacle and hoarding it, and did not pay the zakat and the obligatory dues due upon it; he was preoccupied with it away from the religion, and boasted of possessing it and was arrogant.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 70, verse 19–35:

By "man" (al-insan) is meant mankind, which is why the exception of "those who pray" (al-musallin) is made from it. Al-halaʿ (haloa, extreme anxiety): quick impatience upon touching what is disliked, and quick withholding upon touching good, from the saying "a she-camel that is halwaʿ," meaning swift in her pace. It is related from Ahmad ibn Yahya that Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Tahir said to me: "What is al-halaʿ?" I said: "God has explained it, and there is no explanation clearer than His explanation: it is the one who, when evil befalls him, displays intense distress, and when good reaches him, he begrudges it and withholds it from people."

The "good" is wealth and affluence, and the "evil" is poverty. Or it is health and sickness: when he is healthy and wealthy, he withholds kindness and is stingy with his wealth; and when he falls ill, he becomes distressed and begins to make bequests. The meaning is: man, due to his preference for distress and withholding, and their being firmly established and deeply rooted in him, is as if he were created and naturally disposed to them, and as if it were a innate, necessary matter, not a matter of choice, like His saying ﴿Man was created of haste﴾ [al-Anbiya 21:37]. The proof of this is that when he was in the womb and the cradle, there was no halaʿ in him. Also, it is a blame, and God does not blame His own act. The proof of this is the exception of the believers who struggled against their souls, compelled them to hardships, and restrained them from desires, [Note: "wa-zalfuwha ʿan al-shahawat" — in al-Sihah: "zalafa nafsahu ʿan al-shayʾ," meaning he restrained it from doing or approaching it. (ʿ)] so that they were neither distressed nor withholding. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The worst thing that a son of Adam is given is a greedy, anxious stinginess and a cowardly, anxious fear" [Narrated by Abu Dawud, Ibn Hibban, Ahmad, Ishaq and al-Bazzar, all by way of ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Marwan: I heard Abu Hurayrah with this, but he said "the worst thing in a man"].

If you say: how does He say ﴿who are constant in their prayer﴾ and then ﴿who guard their prayer﴾? I say: the meaning of their constancy in it is that they persist in performing it, not neglecting it, nor occupying themselves away from it with any distractions, as was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The best deed is the most constant, even if it is little" [Agreed upon, from the hadith of ʿAʾishah]. And ʿAʾishah's saying: "His deed was constant" [Agreed upon, from her narration, may God be pleased with her]. Their guarding of it: that they observe the complete ablution for it and its times, establish its pillars, complete it with its sunnah and its etiquettes, and preserve it from being nullified [Mahmud said: "That is, they do not abandon it at any time nor nullify it..." Ahmad said: preserving it from being nullified is a text, according to the People of the Sunnah, of preserving it from disbelief specifically, so that nothing else nullifies it, in contrast to the Qadariyya; similar examples have been mentioned before, and God knows best] by committing sins. So constancy refers to the prayers themselves, and guarding refers to their conditions.

﴿A known right﴾ is zakat, because it is determined and known, or it is a charity that a man imposes upon himself, paying it at known times. "The beggar" (al-sa'il) is the one who asks; and "the deprived" (al-mahrum) is the one who abstains from asking, so he is thought to be wealthy and is thus deprived. ﴿Who affirm the Day of Judgment﴾: affirming it through their deeds and their preparation for it, and they fear the punishment of their Lord.

He interjects with His saying ﴿Indeed, the punishment of their Lord is not to be deemed safe﴾, meaning: no one should feel secure from it, however much he exceeds in obedience and striving; he should be balanced between fear and hope. It was recited: "bi-shahadatihim" and "bi-shahadatatihim" (their testimonies). Testimony is among the trusts, and He singled it out from among them to show its excellence, since upholding it entails the revival and establishment of rights; and to neglect it means its loss and nullification.
